tracks.title: Cold Open: The Human Moment
tracks.text: It's also rewarding. I'm kind of a people person. So I like to talk to people. So it's better than just being in your office or the lab all day.

tracks.title: Name And Title
tracks.text: so my name's Katherine Roche. I'm a senior investigator at National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke at NIH.

tracks.title: Her Work
tracks.text: so I am a basic researcher. And I got my PhD a very long time ago. And I've been working on glutamate receptors really the entire time. But then there was this explosion in human genetics where more and more patient populations were getting sequenced. And it became clear that sometimes there were mutations, single point mutations, in individuals that caused a lot of problems. They were pathogenic. And it turned out that some of these variants are in the proteins I had studied for decades.

tracks.title: The Pivot
tracks.text: And I started off being a very basic scientist and really have pivoted. Our lab almost entirely focuses our research on these rare variants that are found in patient populations. So we primarily study NMDA receptors. And they're encoded by the GRIN genes, in particular GRIN2B and GRIN2A.

tracks.title: What Families Changed
tracks.text: Half my lab studies one class of proteins, which has been known for decades, even before the genetics, the next-gen sequencing, caught up to be important. But there's no advocacy group. And it lags so far behind. I just have parents or providers. They find out online that I've published on it. And they ask me questions. The other half of lab study is GRIN disorders. And it's just the community is hugely important. It gets more research dollars. But also, you learn more.

tracks.title: Small Progress
tracks.text: But really, families would also like to have anything that helps the symptoms. And so small progress is important.

tracks.title: Where It Stands
tracks.text: But I also make the point that even though it's a somewhat complex biological protein and complex of proteins, people have studied it for decades in pharma because everyone knows NMDA receptors are important. So what it has in complexity nicely, it has the counterpart in that there's a lot of pharma companies, biotech companies, that have spent decades. So there's a lot of potential pharmacological interventions that are further along than you might imagine. So there could be short-term therapies, which are still lengthy to come up with, that are more drug-based. And there may be others that actually correct the gene. But those are almost certainly further in the future.

tracks.title: Science Is Slow
tracks.text: I know that parents are frustrated that developing therapies are so slow. Science is slow. Publishing is slow. So if you want to wait for a paper to be published on a particular topic, you may have wasted a year or two trying to embark on something that's already been done.

tracks.title: The Nih Study
tracks.text: That's all changed in the last few months. I'm now associated with the neurogenetics team at NINDS. And this is really fabulous for me and I think for the research and the people that are affected, hopefully, by my research in that we can bring in patients to the clinical center. You would have to get to Bethesda and you'd obviously have to schedule it and all that. But we could collect all the clinical data. The clinicians can take blood samples. They can take skin biopsy. These are important if we want to make cell lines, patient-derived cell lines.

tracks.title: A Research Hospital
tracks.text: So NIH has the largest clinical research hospital in the world. No one pays. They don't even have a billing department. So you would have to get to Bethesda. But if you're brought in under this protocol, which is a very broad protocol looking at genetic disorders, then you could get these analyses. And you could contribute the information and blood samples. And it would all be taken care of. It's not a normal hospital. You wouldn't go to the clinical center if you broke your leg or if you're having a baby. It's a research hospital. So almost every patient that's certainly an inpatient, and even these, you have to be under a protocol. So it's all research associated.

tracks.title: Button
tracks.text: So the direct interaction is incredibly important. And it's made it to where we've expanded our research to try to get tissue and samples from patients. And I don't think we would have ever dreamed to kind of go in that direction if we didn't have such a robust relationship with the GRIN families.
